analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax never got a cosponsor, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal estate tax, which applies only to very large inheritances, along with the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax that together tax large transfers of wealth. Repeal would spare heirs of the biggest estates a tax of up to roughly 40 percent on amounts above the exemption, while reducing federal revenue that someone else would eventually have to make up through other taxes or borrowing. The bill attracted no cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and was never considered.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates would gain the most. In 2013 the estate tax only applied to estates above roughly $5 million per person ($10 million per married couple), so repeal would exclusively benefit families passing on wealth above that line. Wealthy individuals planning to make large lifetime gifts would also gain, since the gift tax would disappear alongside the estate tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, which contains the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, effective for deaths, gifts, and transfers occurring after enactment.
Because these taxes apply only to large estates and transfers, repeal would direct its entire benefit to families inheriting or transferring wealth above the federal exemption threshold.

analysis.who_pays: The general public would bear the cost. The estate tax is one of the most progressive sources of federal revenue, collected almost entirely from multimillion-dollar estates; eliminating it would either add to federal deficits or require higher taxes elsewhere. Repealing the gift tax at the same time would also open a new route to shelter income and wealth from taxation by giving it away tax-free.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate revenue raised almost entirely from the largest estates, shifting the burden onto other taxpayers or adding to deficits.

Repealing the gift tax alongside the estate tax would let wealthy individuals transfer money and property during their lifetime without any tax, a major new avenue for avoiding income and payroll taxes on accumulated wealth.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: families with the largest inheritances would save up to roughly 40 percent on everything above the exemption. The cost is diffuse: federal revenue that currently comes from a few thousand multimillion-dollar estates would have to be replaced by taxes on everyone else or by borrowing. The bill offered no offsetting revenue and no provision for ordinary households, so its costs to the general public outweighed its narrow gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Boozman introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act on July 31, 2013; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over the life of the Congress.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off that it died: the estate tax remained in place, so federal revenue continued to be collected from the largest estates rather than being replaced with broader taxes or deficits. The families with the largest estates, and the advocates of repeal, lost the opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; large estates kept paying

for.name: Sen. John Boozman
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arkansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its sole sponsor; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill and no Democrat cosponsored it; it never reached a vote, so there was no recorded split beyond its one-sided sponsorship.

industries.industry: Heirs and families with the largest estates
industries.note: Repeal would have spared estates above the exemption a tax of up to roughly 40 percent, a benefit flowing exclusively to families inheriting multimillion-dollar wealth, with the revenue made up by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning and trust services (law firms, wealth managers)
industries.note: Estate and gift taxes drive demand for planning services; repeal would have removed the tax but also removed a major driver of high-end wealth-management business, while loosening rules on transferring wealth.
The estate tax is one of the most progressive federal taxes; losing it would shift costs onto the general public through deficits or other taxes.
